title: A Phase 2 Trial of a Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Human Metapneumovirus Combination Virus-Like Particle Vaccine IVX-A12 in Adults ≥60 Years of Age

analysis.research_question_and_background: Older adults (≥60 years) are susceptible to severe outcomes from infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or human metapneumovirus (hMPV). This study aimed to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of a combination vaccine targeting both pathogens.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This Phase 2 trial randomized adults ≥60 years of age to receive a single dose of IVX-A12 (150 μg RSV/150 μg hMPV) or the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3 (120 μg with AS01E adjuvant). Overall, 143 participants were enrolled, with 71 receiving IVX-A12 and 72 receiving RSVPreF3.
analysis.methods: Safety and immunogenicity were evaluated through 180 days post-vaccination. Solicited adverse reactions were monitored through Day 7, while unsolicited adverse events were collected through Day 29. Serious adverse events and medically attended adverse events were documented through Day 181.
analysis.main_results: Solicited adverse reactions occurred in 25 (35.2%) participants receiving IVX-A12 and 36 (50.0%) receiving RSVPreF3. Unsolicited adverse events were reported in 5 (7.0%) and 11 (15.3%) participants, respectively. Serious adverse events were observed in 2 (2.8%) and 1 (1.4%) participants, while medically attended adverse events were reported in 1 (1.4%) and 9 (12.5%) participants.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 were well tolerated and elicited neutralizing antibody responses against their targeted pathogens. Notably, IVX-A12 also increased neutralizing antibody levels against hMPV A and B, which was not observed with RSVPreF3.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that IVX-A12 may offer broader protection against both RSV and hMPV, which could inform future vaccine development and public health strategies for older adults at risk of severe respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to a single dose and short follow-up period, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the safety assessments and the lack of long-term efficacy data.

analysis.summary_en: This Phase 2 trial evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of IVX-A12, a combination vaccine targeting respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), in adults ≥60 years of age. The study compared IVX-A12 with the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3. Both vaccines were well tolerated, with similar rates of solicited adverse reactions but lower rates of unsolicited events with IVX-A12. IVX-A12 elicited neutralizing antibody responses against both RSV and hMPV, while RSVPreF3 only targeted RSV. The results suggest that IVX-A12 may provide broader protection against hMPV, which is relevant for vaccine development and public health strategies in older adults. However, the study's short duration and single-dose regimen limit the confidence in its findings, and further research is needed to assess long-term efficacy and safety.

title: Diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses in children: comparison with a multiplex PCR panel and correlation with viral load.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize how the sensitivity of rapid antigen tests for respiratory viruses is influenced by viral load, particularly for human metapneumovirus (hMPV). The sensitivity of these tests relative to PCR-based testing has been incompletely characterized.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This prospective, paired-specimen study was conducted at a pediatric center, where two simultaneous nasopharyngeal swabs were obtained from children with respiratory tract infections (RTI). A total of 1,584 paired specimens from 1,232 children (median age: 3.0 years [IQR: 1.0–6.0]; 53.7% male) were analyzed.
analysis.methods: Specimens positive by either the antigen-based rapid test kits or the multiplex PCR panel underwent confirmatory quantitative real-time PCR to determine viral load. The study evaluated antigen tests for six common pediatric respiratory viruses, including hMPV, against a multiplex PCR reference standard across 1,584 clinical specimens.
analysis.main_results: Sensitivity of the antigen tests ranged from 20.6% (adenovirus) to 79.7% (hMPV), while specificity exceeded 99% for all six targets and overall agreement ranged from 90.7% to 99.0%. For every virus, antigen test positivity increased steeply with viral load, approaching 90–100% at viral loads ≥10^6–10^7 copies/100 μL and falling below 50% at loads ≤10^4–10^5 copies/100 μL.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings clarify the clinical role of rapid antigen testing, showing that it reliably identifies children with the highest viral burden, who are most likely to have acute, symptomatic infection warranting immediate clinical action.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the use of antigen testing in identifying children with high viral loads of hMPV, which can inform clinical decision-making and prioritize interventions for those with acute, symptomatic infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is based on a single center and may not be generalizable to other populations. The evidence strength is moderate, as the results are based on a well-characterized paired-specimen design with a clear link to viral load.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses, including human metapneumovirus (hMPV), in children. The research aimed to understand how sensitivity varies with viral load, as this relationship has not been fully characterized. The study was conducted at a pediatric center using paired nasopharyngeal swabs, with one tested by rapid antigen tests and the other by a multiplex PCR panel. Sensitivity of the antigen tests ranged from 20.6% for adenovirus to 79.7% for hMPV, with high specificity across all targets. Antigen test positivity increased with viral load, reaching 90–100% at high loads (≥10^6–10^7 copies/100 μL) and dropping below 50% at lower loads. The results suggest that antigen testing is effective in identifying children with high viral burdens, who are most likely to have acute, symptomatic infections. However, the study's findings are limited by its single-center design and may not be generalizable to other populations. The evidence strength is moderate due to the clear methodology and direct correlation with viral load.

title: The MSC–RSV/HMPV interface: impacts on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and risk of non-atopic asthma and COPD

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the impact of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) infection on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and the risk of non-atopic asthma and COPD. It explores the role of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) in tissue repair and immune response modulation following HMPV infection.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It includes general background information on HMPV and its association with respiratory infections, particularly in children and adults.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: There is consensus that HMPV is a significant etiologic agent of respiratory tract infections, especially in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life are associated with histopathological damage and may increase the risk of chronic pulmonary diseases like non-atopic asthma. In adults, HMPV exacerbates respiratory symptoms and contributes to chronic inflammation in individuals with COPD.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights the potential for HMPV to infect MSCs, which may affect their immunomodulatory capacity and plasticity, thereby influencing tissue renewal. However, the evidence is limited and does not provide a clear consensus on the mechanisms or outcomes of this interaction. There is a lack of detailed studies on the long-term effects of HMPV on lung tissue and the specific role of MSCs in recovery.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to understand the molecular mechanisms by which HMPV affects MSC function and to explore the potential of MSC-based therapies in mitigating lung damage and chronic disease progression. Clinical studies should focus on the long-term outcomes of HMPV infections and their impact on respiratory health.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines the role of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) in respiratory tract infections and its potential impact on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and the development of chronic diseases such as non-atopic asthma and COPD. It highlights the involvement of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) in tissue repair and immune response modulation following HMPV infection. While there is agreement on the clinical burden of HMPV, particularly in children and adults with COPD, the evidence is limited regarding the specific effects of HMPV on MSCs and the long-term consequences of infection. The review suggests that future research should focus on elucidating the mechanisms of MSC interaction with HMPV and the potential for MSC-based interventions in managing respiratory diseases.

title: Respiratory Pathogens Detected among Pediatric Hospitalizations for Pneumonia: A Multicenter Study from Saitama, Japan.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of routine in-hospital testing in detecting respiratory pathogens in children with pneumonia, highlighting the need for more comprehensive diagnostic methods.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prefecture-wide multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted at four hospitals in Saitama, Japan, from July 2023 to March 2024, involving 1,170 pediatric hospitalizations for acute respiratory infections (ARIs), of which 457 were complicated by pneumonia.
analysis.methods: Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was used to detect respiratory pathogens, with 199 hospitalizations undergoing this test. Additionally, in 123 hospitalizations where routine tests were negative, multiplex PCR identified pathogens in 85 cases.
analysis.main_results: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV; n=124, 27.1%) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; n=85, 18.6%) were the most frequently detected pathogens among the 457 pneumonia cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrated that multiplex PCR significantly enhances pathogen detection beyond routine testing, providing a broader spectrum of identifiable respiratory pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that implementing multiplex PCR in diagnostic protocols could improve the accuracy of pathogen identification in pediatric pneumonia cases, aiding in targeted treatment and surveillance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and comprehensive testing methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the detection of respiratory pathogens in children hospitalized with pneumonia in Saitama, Japan, using a multicenter retrospective cohort design. Routine in-hospital testing was found insufficient, as multiplex PCR identified additional pathogens in cases where routine tests were negative. The most frequently detected pathogens were human metapneumovirus (hMPV) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The study highlights the value of multiplex PCR in improving diagnostic accuracy, which could have important implications for clinical management and public health surveillance. However, the retrospective nature of the study and potential biases may limit the generalizability of the findings. The evidence is considered strong due to the large sample size and the use of advanced molecular testing methods.

title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections

analysis.scope_and_question: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infection and disease. The review focuses on the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of HMPV-associated respiratory infections, particularly in vulnerable populations such as young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on HMPV infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Human metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against HMPV remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) infections, emphasizing its impact on vulnerable populations. The evidence highlights the virus's targeting of respiratory epithelium and the immune responses it triggers. While investigational therapies like fusion and protease inhibitors show promise, their efficacy remains unproven. Vaccine development is ongoing, with several candidates in early stages. The review underscores the need for further clinical trials, improved diagnostics, and public awareness to address the public health burden of HMPV. Despite the lack of specific treatments and vaccines, the study suggests that emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions.

title: Human Metapneumovirus Nucleoprotein Impairs Stress-Induced Mitophagy and Mitochondrial Quality Control

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is an important respiratory pathogen for which specific antiviral therapies are currently unavailable, and the mechanisms by which HMPV regulates host mitochondrial homeostasis remain poorly understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we investigated the role of HMPV nucleoprotein (N) in mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial quality control, with a focus on its association with selective autophagy-related factors.
analysis.methods: Using recombinant protein purification, surface plasmon resonance, co-immunoprecipitation, confocal microscopy, mitochondrial-targeted mitophagy reporter analysis, and immunoblotting, we examined the interaction between HMPV N and host autophagy-associated factors and evaluated its effects on mitophagy.
analysis.main_results: We demonstrated that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, two key components of the selective autophagy machinery.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: HMPV N signals were spatially associated with mitochondrial regions, and HMPV N expression increased the spatial association of TAX1BP1-positive structures with mitochondria, while reducing the spatial association of LC3-positive structures with TOM20-positive mitochondria under stress conditions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Consistently, HMPV N expression reduced CCCP-induced mitochondrial delivery to acidic compartments and attenuated TOM20 degradation, while exerting limited effects on basal mitochondrial turnover.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: These findings identify HMPV N as a viral regulator of stress-induced mitophagy and suggest that its interactions with selective autophagy-associated factors contribute to altered mitochondrial homeostasis during infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of HMPV nucleoprotein (N) in mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial quality control. The research aims to understand how HMPV affects host mitochondrial homeostasis, a poorly characterized area. Using a range of molecular and cellular techniques, the study demonstrates that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, key components of the selective autophagy machinery. The results show that HMPV N expression increases the spatial association of TAX1BP1-positive structures with mitochondria while reducing the association of LC3-positive structures with TOM20-positive mitochondria under stress conditions. These findings suggest that HMPV N modulates stress-induced mitophagy through interactions with autophagy-related factors, potentially contributing to altered mitochondrial homeostasis during infection. The study provides insights into the molecular mechanisms of HMPV pathogenesis, which could inform future research on antiviral strategies and mitochondrial-targeted therapies. However, the study is limited to in vitro and cell-based experiments, which may not fully represent in vivo conditions. The evidence is strong based on the experimental methods and results, but further studies are needed to validate these findings in clinical settings.

title: Coinfections With Respiratory Syncytial Virus in a Cohort of Adults With High‐Risk Conditions, 2015–2020: A Retrospective Observational Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate RSV coinfections in high-risk adults, addressing a knowledge gap regarding the significance of RSV coinfections in this population, which may be at increased risk for severe infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study of 3601 respiratory samples from adults with high-risk conditions over five winter seasons from 2015 to 2020, focusing on RSV coinfections.
analysis.methods: Residual respiratory specimens from community-dwelling adults with ≥1 high-risk conditions were retested using a multiplex panel for multiple viral pathogens, with RSV coinfection defined as detection of ≥2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non-RSV.
analysis.main_results: RSV was detected in 303 (8.4%) of 3601 samples, with 5.9% of RSV-positive adults having coinfections, primarily with rhinovirus (RV) and influenza virus (IFV).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that RSV coinfections were most common with RV and IFV, and there were no statistically significant differences between coinfections and single infections according to high-risk conditions, potentially due to limited statistical power.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that RSV coinfections may be associated with increased disease severity in high-risk adults, highlighting the need for further research and surveillance in this population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had a relatively small sample size and low number of RSV coinfections detected, limiting the ability to detect differences between coinfections and single infections. The study period was before the COVID-19 pandemic and did not include coinfections with SARS-CoV-2.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated RSV coinfections in high-risk adults, finding that 5.9% of RSV-positive adults had coinfections, primarily with rhinovirus and influenza virus. The findings suggest a need for further research and surveillance in this population.

title: Predictive modelling to differentiate possible bacterial and viral cases of childhood pneumonia in Kilifi, Kenya using protein markers and clinical data

analysis.research_question_and_background: We aimed to incorporate a wide range of novel biomarkers and clinical presentations into a multivariable model and to validate its ability to differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia.MethodsA total of 457 children aged 2–59 months, admitted to the Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Kenya, with WHO defined pneumonia were classified using gold standard laboratory diagnostics as possible bacterial (i.e., bacterial/ unknown cases, n = 229) or possible viral (n = 228) infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%).
analysis.methods: DiscussionIn this nested case-control study, we utilized a dataset containing data on a wide range of clinical signs and symptoms, complete blood cell counts, CRP, PCT and 6 novel biomarker levels to develop a multivariable predictive model and evaluate its ability to discriminate between bacterial and viral pneumonia in children presenting with WHO-defined pneumonia.
analysis.main_results: This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The model demonstrated fair, but inadequate, discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.61.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Diagnostic tools to guide the rational use of antibiotics in the treatment of pneumonia are needed.The distinction between bacterial and viral pneumonia remains challenging, especially in Low- and Middle-Income countries (LMICs).
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This analysis follows the widespread administration of the PCV and Hib vaccines in Kenya; in this context, the case mix presentating to the hospital is increasingly of viral etiology and therefore would not benefit from antibiotics.

analysis.summary_en: We aimed to incorporate a wide range of novel biomarkers and clinical presentations into a multivariable model and to validate its ability to differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia.MethodsA total of 457 children aged 2–59 months, admitted to the Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Kenya, with WHO defined pneumonia were classified using gold standard laboratory diagnostics as possible bacterial (i.e., bacterial/ unknown cases, n = 229) or possible viral (n = 228) infections. The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%). DiscussionIn this nested case-control study, we utilized a dataset containing data on a wide range of clinical signs and symptoms, complete blood cell counts, CRP, PCT and 6 novel biomarker levels to develop a multivariable predictive model and evaluate its ability to discriminate between bacterial and viral pneumonia in children presenting with WHO-defined pneumonia. This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management. The model demonstrated fair, but inadequate, discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.61. Diagnostic tools to guide the rational use of antibiotics in the treatment of pneumonia are needed.The distinction between bacterial and viral pneumonia remains challenging, especially in Low- and Middle-Income countries (LMICs).
